# Autonomous cryoprotectant loading of the oocyte using microfluidic transistors

**Authors:** Li Zhan; Hunter Hinnen; Kaustav A. Gopinathan; Mehmet Toner

**Affiliations:** 1 Center for Engineering in Medicine and Surgery, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 2 Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 3 Department of Electrical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA | 4 Shriners Children, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Oocyte cryopreservation is a critical step of in vitro fertilization (IVF). The handling and loading of cryoprotectant currently rely on manual pipetting methods, which leads to outcome variations, high cost and limited accessibility. Here we developed a low-cost and user-friendly microfluidic device to automate the complex multistep process of oocyte CPA loading, delivering cryopreservation-ready oocytes. We utilized microfluidic transistors to create fluidic timers and logic gates, which generated time-dependent pressure signals to control the embedded valves, thereby regulating the flow conditions over the oocyte. Using constant pressure supplies, we demonstrated autonomous mouse oocyte trapping, linear loading of equilibrium solution, dehydration with vitrification solution and oocyte extraction from the device. Our work represents an important step towards autonomous IVF-on-a-chip to enhance the accessibility and affordability of IVF.

## Introduction

Approximately 1 in 6 adults worldwide experience infertility, with a lifetime infertility prevalence of 17.8% in high-income countries and 16.5% in low- and middle-income countries, as indicated in a 2023 WHO report.1 Assisted reproductive technologies, such as in vitro fertilization (IVF), have revolutionized the landscape of reproductive medicine since the first successful live human birth by IVF in 1978.2–7 The typical IVF process involves ovarian stimulation, oocyte retrieval, fertilization through intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), embryo culture, and finally embryo transfer into the uterus. Oocyte cryopreservation involves storing oocytes in a suspended state at cryogenic temperatures (i.e., in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C). As multiple oocytes can be retrieved in a single cycle, oocyte cryopreservation has been established as an essential component for infertility treatment.8,9 Furthermore, it enables donor oocyte banking and fertility preservation for women who are at risk of losing their ovarian functions due to cancer treatments and/or plan to delay pregnancy.

Cryopreservation by vitrification involves cooling of a liquid substance to an amorphous glassy state without the destructive formation of ice crystals.10–13 To achieve successful vitrification, fast cooling rates and loading of high concentration glass-forming cryoprotectant agents (CPAs) into cytoplasm are usually required. Notably, both osmotic stress and CPA toxicity can lead to cell damage.14,15 Therefore, the CPA loading protocol plays a pivotal role in the outcome of cryopreservation. During CPA loading, the oocytes first shrink to a minimal volume due to high water permeability upon initial exposure to CPA solution of high osmolarity, then swell back as CPA and water slowly re-enter the oocyte. To mitigate excess cell shrinkage caused by osmotic stress, multistep CPA loading protocols can be performed to allow the cell to shrink in stages.13,16,17 For instance, oocytes are manually transferred between several CPA droplets (i.e., 50 μL) of increasing concentrations under a microscope to avoid any cell loss. After reaching the equilibrium solution (ES) which is 7.5% ethylene glycol (EG) + 7.5% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), the oocytes are transferred to a droplet of vitrification solution (VS, 15% EG + 15% DMSO + 0.5 M sucrose) for dehydration over a brief period (i.e., <90 seconds), then placed onto a device (i.e., Cryotop, Cryoloop, quartz capillary etc.) with minimal volume, and rapidly plunged into liquid nitrogen for cooling.12,18–20 In addition, the time duration of each step needs to be precisely followed because CPA toxicity increases with time, especially at high concentrations. Currently, the time-consuming and tedious CPA loading is manually conducted by skilled embryologists after multiple years of training. Importantly, manual handling lacks precise control of oocytes CPA loading (i.e., solution carryover between droplets) and suffers from operator-to-operator variability, leading to inconsistent outcomes for precious reproductive cells. This underscores the urgent need to improve the oocyte CPA loading protocol and reduce the influence of operators.

Compared with manual pipetting, microfluidics offers opportunities to enable precise control over CPA concentration around the oocyte and minimize the operator-to-operator variability.21–23 Heo et al. demonstrated microfluidic ES loading with a linear concentration profile created by syringe pumps to substantially reduce osmotic stress and cell shrinkage.24 However, their system was not designed to extract the oocyte from the device. Lai et al. developed a microfluidic device that enabled linear ES loading, VS dehydration and oocyte extraction.25 Their results showed that linear ES loading resulted in higher cytoplasmic lipid retention and improved developmental competence in bovine and murine models, compared to traditional step ES loading. Nevertheless, multiple syringe pumps were used, and manual switching of different solutions was required, limiting clinical translation. Commercial products such as DaVitri (Overture) enable programmable CPA loading but require highly skilled personnel to reliably transfer the CPA-loaded oocyte with a fine tip instrument prior to vitrification.26,27 Alternatively, robotics were employed to automate the liquid handling. For instance, Zhang et al. reported a pick-and-place platform using visual detection algorithms and sophisticated robotic systems.28 Gavi (Genea Biomedx) employs consumable chip that automatically loads CPA and serves as vitrification carrier to minimize egg relocation.29,30 However, low cooling rates are expected and can potentially lead to compromised survival after cryopreservation. The widespread clinical adoption of robotic systems is hindered by the cost-effectiveness and special training requirement. Thus, new innovations are required to achieve autonomous CPA loading to deliver vitrification-ready oocytes. Critically, these devices must be simple and low-cost to facilitate clinical translation, even in resource-limited settings.

In our previous work, we developed a microfluidic transistor for autonomous liquid handling.31 The technology enabled the creation of autonomous microfluidic circuits that function like classic electronic circuits but operate entirely on fluidic signals. A microfluidic transistor consists of two crossed fluid channels separated by a deformable membrane. Pressure differences across the membrane can induce nonlinear flow-limitation effects in the channels, closely analogous to the saturation behavior of the electronic transistor. A wide range of both fundamental and complex electronic circuit designs have been demonstrated directly in the microfluidic domain. These fluidic circuits are fully self-contained within the microfluidic chip and can be integrated with functional microfluidic elements (i.e., traps, droplet generators etc.) to process liquid and biologics automatically without any external optical or electronic sensors.

In this work, we present a simple and low-cost microfluidic device to achieve autonomous oocyte trapping, linear ES loading, VS dehydration and oocyte extraction, enabling one-touch preparation of vitrification-ready oocytes. Using microfluidic transistor technology, we created fluid timers with long durations (> 15 minutes) and generated time-dependent digital pressure outputs with fluidic logic gates. These digital pressure outputs control the opening and closing of embedded valves, therefore allowing precise regulation of flow conditions over the oocyte. In addition, we demonstrated the capability to produce linear ES concentration over desired time using the fluidic capacitor. Once the oocyte was loaded into the device, the sequential delivery of different solutions at designated timepoints occurred automatically, without human intervention, bulky syringe pumps or electronics. Finally, we successfully extracted the CPA-loaded oocyte from the device, highlighting the robustness of our technology.

## Results

### Design of the microfluidic device

To design an autonomous microfluidic device for preparing vitrification-ready oocytes, three key processes need to be accomplished in the following sequence. The first step is trapping and holding the oocyte within the device. This ensures accurate and robust delivery of subsequent CPA solutions. The second step is gradually loading the oocyte with ES in a linear concentration manner to minimize cell shrinkage. The final step is dehydrating the oocyte with high concentration VS and collecting the vitrification-ready oocyte. This step requires limiting the exposure time of oocyte to VS to reduce toxicity, while ensuring extraction of the oocyte from the device.

We developed two chips, the oocyte chip (i.e., the actuator) and the microfluidic transistor chip (i.e., the controller), to execute the multi-step protocol (Figure 1). Specifically, the oocyte chip directly interacts with the oocyte and handles the various solutions used throughout the process. As shown in Figures. 1 and 2A, the oocyte chip includes three inlets: 1) inlet for oocyte to enter the chip, 2) inlet for ES and media to generate a linear concentration profile, and 3) inlet for VS to dehydrate the oocyte and meanwhile expel the oocyte out of the chip for collection. In addition, there are two outlets: one for oocyte collection and one for liquid waste. To facilitate the sequential flow of various solutions through the oocyte chip, four sets of hydraulic Quake-style valves are placed at the inlet for oocyte (valve A), inlet for ES and media (valve B), inlet for VS & outlet for oocyte collection (valve C), and outlet for liquid waste (valve D, Figure 2A). A detailed schematic of the oocyte chip is presented in Figure S1. The operational status (i.e., open or closed) of these valves and time durations of the three-step process are listed in Figure 2B. For instance, from 200 to 1100 seconds, valves A and C are closed, while valves B and D are open to gradually load ES into the trapped oocyte. These Quake-style valves are fabricated by sandwiching a thin silicone membrane between the inlet/outlet channel of the oocyte chip and the corresponding control channel connected to the microfluidic transistor chip (Figure S2).

To control the valves, we designed a microfluidic transistor chip to generate four time-dependent digital pressure signals from constant pressure supplies. The microfluidic transistor chip contains three fluidic timers with durations of 200, 1100 and 1175 seconds. The output pressure of these timers is fed to four fluidic logic gates to produce digital pressure signals that alternate between high and low pressure at designated time points. These digital pressure outputs are employed to open and close the valves A, B, C and D, thereby managing the flow of various solutions in the oocyte chip. For instance, as illustrated in Figure. S2, when the pressure of port C from the transistor chip is low, vale C is opened, allowing VS to flow into the oocyte chip. In addition, the fluid in the transistor chip and oocyte chip is separated by the silicone membrane of the valves.

### Developing long duration fluidic timer with the microfluidic transistor

We constructed the fluidic timer by combining a RC low-pass filter and an inverter (Figure 3A). As the supply pressure (Psup1) increases from 0 to 200 kPa, the low pass filter creates a fixed time of delay in the rise of capacitor pressure (PC), which triggers the inverter and causes the output pressure (Pout) to drop. The microfluidic channel layout is presented in Figure 3A, with a 20 μm thickness silicone membrane sandwiched between two PDMS layers (green and pink in Figure 3A). Two microfluidic transistors (blue in Figure 3A) are used in this timer circuit. Air inside a rigid container (i.e., a syringe with the plunger glued to the syringe wall) is used as the capacitor. When the capacitor syringe is connected to the microfluidic circuit, increasing pressure at the connection point drives liquid into the syringe, which compresses the air inside and raises the air pressure until equilibrium is reached (Figure 3B). The capacitance C can be calculated as C = dV/dP, where V and P are the liquid volume and pressure inside the capacitor syringe, respectively. As presented in Figure 3B, the model that accounts for the time-dependent capacitance demonstrates a better match with experimental measurement of PC, compared to the constant capacitance model (details in Method section).

As PC exceeds the supply pressure for the inverter (Psup2, 180 kPa), the output pressure (Pout) decreases from 175 kPa to 11 kPa. By increasing the air volume in the capacitor syringe from 0.1 mL to 2 mL and 4 mL, we demonstrated timer durations of 63, 584 and 1237 seconds, respectively. Figure 3C depicts the overlay of three experimental repeats, highlighting robust performance of our fluidic timer. Additionally, with constant pressure supplies (Psup1 and Psup2), the model indicates that the timer duration is proportional to the initial air volume in capacitor syringe and the resistor R1. Indeed, as we varied the air volume from 0.1 mL to 4 mL, we observed a linear increase of timer from 63 to 1237 seconds (Figure 3D). We selected 0.6 mL, 3.7 mL and 3.9 mL air volume to create fluidic timers of 200, 1100 and 1175 seconds as needed in our application (Figure 2B). Further, in this work, we focus on the timer circuit that can achieve long durations (i.e., > 15 minutes) for CPA loading applications. Regarding short durations (i.e., 6 seconds), a different timer circuit has been demonstrated in our previous work.31

### Generating time-dependent digital pressure signal using fluidic logic gates

Having demonstrated the fluidic timer that triggers a state change of the output pressure at designated timepoint, we next integrated logic gate circuits to generate time-dependent pressure states for controlling valves in the oocyte chip. Specifically, as shown in Figure 4A, the inputs to the logic gates are the outputs of three timer circuits, denoted as P1, P2, and P3. which change states from 1 to 0 (i.e., high pressure to low pressure) at 1100, 200, and 1175 seconds, respectively. The logic gate outputs are the required status of valve A, B, C, and D in the multi-step protocol, where 1 represents high pressure to close the valve and 0 represents low pressure to open the valve (Figure 4). To achieve the desired outputs, we used Karnaugh mapping and NAND simplification, resulting in a circuit with four logic gates including two NOT and two NAND gates, as illustrated in Figure 4B.

As illustrated in the integrated electrical schematic diagram (Figure 4C), we employed two pressure supplies to drive three fluidic timers and one pressure supply to drive four fluidic logic gates, all connected to the common ground. A total of 18 microfluidic transistors, along with 4 fluidic resistors and 3 fluidic capacitors, work together to compute 4 digital pressure outputs, entirely without electronics. Notably, our approach is highly scalable, allowing us to generate copious functional digital pressure outputs with additional fluidic computing components. To translate the electrical diagram to the fluidic domain, we fabricated a 4-layer PDMS device (detailed schematic diagram for fabrication in Figure S3). As illustrated in Figure 4D, in addition to the layer 1 (green) and layer 2 (pink) microchannels which create microfluidic transistors (blue), we included two routing layers to prevent undesired microchannel crossings. The layer 0 (red), positioned above layer 1, bridges ports with shared pressure supplies and ground, while layer 3 (gray), beneath layer 2, feeds the timer circuit outputs to the logic gates.

The fully assembled microfluidic transistor chip filled with green dye is presented in Figure 4E, with an overall size of 4.5 cm by 3.5 cm. Once connected to pressure supplies and external capacitor syringes, the device automatically produces time dependent digital pressure outputs as demonstrated in Figure 4F. For instance, pressure A stays low (i.e., < 20 kPa) for the first 200 seconds and rises to high (i.e., > 140 kPa) at 200 seconds and remains high afterwards. In the oocyte chip, this indicates that valve A is open for the first 200 seconds to allow oocyte loading and trapping, and remains closed after 200 seconds. Moreover, we showed the ability to alternate output pressure state multiple times. In Figure 4F, pressure B starts high for the first 200 seconds, drops to low at 200 seconds and remains low for the next 900 seconds, and eventually switches back to high after 1100 seconds. This sequence commands valve B of the oocyte chip to open only between 200 seconds to 1100 seconds for linear ES loading into the oocyte, while remain closed during oocyte loading (< 200 seconds) and VS loading & oocyte extraction (1100 – 1175 seconds). After 1175 seconds, all output pressures stay high, closing all the valves to stop any flow within the oocyte chip. Note that the first 25 seconds of the pressure curves in Figure 4F reflect the transition phase as the pressure supplies gradually ramp up.

### Optimizing the oocyte trap and linear CPA concentration profile

Two key functionalities of the oocyte chip are trapping the oocyte securely within the device and generating a linear CPA concentration profile. To trap the oocyte, the U-shaped oocyte trap is connected directly to waste outlet via a narrow and short (i.e., 10 μm wide, 15 μm long) microchannel, designed to offer lower fluidic resistance than the alternative route to waste outlet (i.e., 1:4 ratio, Figures 5A). The detailed dimensions of the oocyte trap are included in Figure S4. The distribution of flow streamlines from simulation confirmed the preferrable flow path through the trap (Figure S5). In addition, the narrow microchannel prevents the highly deformable oocyte from squeezing through the trap. To reduce the oocyte loading time, we transfer the oocyte directly into tubing (0.03-inch inner diameter) connected to the inlet port of the oocyte chip (details in the Methods). By adjusting the inlet flow rate to 90 μL/min, we successfully loaded and trapped the oocyte within 2 minutes. However, the high flow rate in the oocyte trap pushes a portion of the oocyte through the narrow channel, causing severe deformation (Figure S6). To address this, we added a parallel siphoning channel connected to the oocyte inlet pathway (i.e., prior to the oocyte trap) through 43 small channels (15 μm wide and 175 μm long, Figure S7), which slows down the flow by 25-fold as indicated by the numerical simulation. In addition, the siphoning channel pushes the oocytes towards the side wall closer to the oocyte trap. With this modification, we showed that the oocyte can be quickly loaded into the chip and successfully trapped without deformation (n=15 experimental replicates, Figure 5A).

In addition to its application in the timer circuit for control of fluids, the RC low pass filter was utilized to create a linearly increasing flow rate of ES, as the result of capacitor charging (Figure 5B). The resistor R4 and capacitor C4 were tuned to ensure that the 900-second linear ES loading occurred within the linear region of the varying capacitance model of the RC circuit (Figure 3B). In the oocyte chip, ES and media meet at a T-junction and enter the serpentine mixing channel with 80 turns, before flowing over the oocyte for CPA loading (Figures 5A–B). We added fluorescent dye (i.e., Rhodamine B) to the media to confirm uniform mixing of ES and media due to Dean flow (i.e., flow vortexes generated in a curved channel) after 49 turns, as indicated by the fluorescent intensity (Figures 5C, S8).

The CPA concentration flowing over the oocyte is determined by the flow rate ratio of ES to media. Notably, the resistance of the serpentine mixer is determined by this flow rate ratio, which changes over time and, in turn, affects the flow rate of both ES and media. To better estimate these flow rates, we analyzed this complex circuit using an analog circuit simulator (details in Method). As suggested by the model, when valve B opens at 200 seconds, media flows through the T-junction to the capacitor syringe, resulting in negative ES flow rates, as confirmed by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5E. This negative ES flow rate delays the onset of linear ES loading and reduces the actual CPA loading time. In addition, as the pressure increases at the T-junction, the model indicates a slight decrease in media flow rate, which is supported by experimental measurement in Figure 5F. We tuned the resistances and capacitance to achieve a linear increase in ES flow rate over time and a final flow ES to media rate ratio of 1:1 at 15 minutes (Figures 5E–F).

### Autonomous CPA loading of the mouse oocyte

We integrated the oocyte chip with the microfluidic transistor chip to achieve fully autonomous oocyte trapping, linear ES loading, oocyte dehydration with VS, and oocyte extraction from the device. By connecting the outputs of the microfluidic transistor chip to automatically control the valves A, B, C and D, we measured the flow rates of each inlet and outlet of the oocyte chip. For the oocyte chip, solely one pressure supply is needed to drive the complex flow of four distinct solutions. As shown in Figure 5D, the oocyte inlet flow rate remains at 90 μL/min only for the first 200 seconds, allowing sufficient time to load and trap the oocyte. Subsequently, the flow from ES and media inlets is activated to enable linear CPA loading between 200 seconds and 1100 seconds (Figures 5E–F). Afterward, the flow to the waste outlet is stopped, and the flow from VS inlet is turned on for dehydration and oocyte collection from 1100 seconds to 1175 seconds. Finally, all valves are closed, with no active flow in the oocyte chip. Overall, we demonstrated successful control of each valve and achieved desired flow conditions throughout the multi-step protocol.

We validated our integrated device with mouse oocyte. After transferring the mouse oocyte to the inlet tubing, the entire process proceeded automatically without human intervention and delivered vitrification-ready oocytes. We performed step loading and linear loading of ES (i.e., 7.5% EG + 7.5% DMSO) separately and compared the volume change of mouse oocytes by recording the entire process using an upright microscope (Supplementary videos 1–2). During the 15 min loading of ES, fluorescent image confirmed that the ES flowed over the oocyte and was not blocked by the trapped oocyte, ensuring sufficient mass transport (Figure S9). In addition, we showed that traditional step loading induced sudden and substantial oocyte shrinkage due to osmotic shock, while the linear loading produced a much more gradual and milder volume change (Figure 5H). The rate of shrinkage (i.e., % of initial volume per second) during linear loading is 0.077 ± 0.009 %/s, which is 44-fold lower than that of step loading, 3.4 ± 0.7 %/s. Additionally, the minimal oocyte volume (% of initial volume) with step loading and linear loading was 62.3 ± 1.7% and 88.1 ± 3.1% respectively (Figure 5I). As presented in Figure 5I, we observed that plasma membrane of oocyte underwent collapsing/folding during step loading, which can potentially cause structural damage. Indeed, we observed the blebbing of oocytes (i.e., 2 out of 5 oocytes) during step loading (Figure S10). In contrast, no blebbing occurred during linear loading (n=5). Further, to demonstrate the versatility of our device, we performed a 10-min linear loading of ES, resulting in a shrinkage rate of 0.13 ± 0.04 %/s, minimal volume of 74.2 ± 1.5 % and no blebbing (n=5, Figure S11). We successfully collected the vitrification-ready oocytes from the device (n=15). The morphology of the shrunken oocyte after exposure to VS is presented in Figure S12. Moreover, we observed intact cell membrane and normal spindle structures in different groups of oocytes including control, 15 min step ES loading, and 15 min linear ES loading (Figure S13).

## Conclusions and Outlook

We report a low cost and user-friendly microfluidic device to automate the multi-step oocyte CPA loading. We showed that linear ES loading can be accomplished using the fluidic capacitor, without electronics or syringe pumps. During initial exposure to the CPA solution, the rate of cell volume shrinkage is proportional to cell surface area and osmolality difference.32,33 Notably, the surface area of oocytes is approximately 100-fold larger than most somatic cells. Conventional step loading exerts high compressive strain rates and induces buckling of the delicate oocyte membrane, which has been related to membrane damage and potentially compromised developmental competence.25,34,35 In addition, the use of microfluidic transistors ensures that only constant pressure supplies are required to operate our device. Automating oocyte CPA loading improves standardization, minimizes variability and reduces cost in this highly sensitive process where 100% recovery of valuable gametes is essential. Further, our ease-to-use technology can enhance the accessibility of IVF treatment by enabling oocyte vitrification in satellite clinics and/or remote settings, rather than solely in embryology labs. This would allow safe transport of oocytes to central embryology labs for fertilization or to long-term storage facilities for preservation.

Over the past four decades, advances in laboratory technologies and equipment have improved human IVF outcomes. Within United States, approximately 2% newborns are conceived through IVF and other assistance reproductive technologies, while the infertility prevalence is as high as ~17%.1 The widespread use of IVF is mainly limited by accessibility and affordability. The high cost of IVF is driven by the need for expensive embryology laboratories and highly trained embryologists.36–39 Moreover, IVF clinics are often located in densely populated urban areas, rendering it difficult for individuals in resource-limited regions to receive timely treatment. From a technology standpoint, current practice involves multistep, labor-intensive, technically challenging manual processes undertaken by skilled professionals, which are subject to human errors and variations. To sustain the exponential demand for IVF, critical advances such as improving efficiency and standardization can be achieved by integrating numerous laboratory handling of gametes/embryos into a streamlined and automated procedure. This could pave the way towards decreased cost and increased accessibility, therefore enabling de-centralization of IVF clinics to benefit a broader population.

Microfluidics can help streamline and automate IVF procedures.23,40–43 Our microfluidic transistor technology can expand this toolbox by enabling on-chip fluidic computation (Supplemental Note S1). For example, several improvements to our current device can be conducted to facilitate clinical translation. Instead of passively waiting for 200 seconds to trap the oocyte, actively detecting the trap of an oocyte through backpressure can be included to facilitate seamless operations. Multiplexing the design to handle more oocytes can also enhance efficiency. Validation with fresh mouse or bovine oocytes needs to be performed and compared with manual pipetting method to evaluate oocyte survival and further developmental competence after ICSI. With the ability to autonomously sense and actuate complex sequences of fluidic events in a scalable and low-cost manner, our approach holds promise towards IVF-on-a chip by automating many other key steps such as oocyte denudation, ICSI, embryo culture and cryopreservation.

## Methods

### Device fabrication

The oocyte chip and microfluidic transistor chip were fabricated using standard PDMS soft lithography techniques. SU-8 negative photoresist (Microchem, USA) was spinned onto a silicon wafer and patterned using UV photolithography to define the master for the chip. The feature dimensions were measured using a surface profilometer (Veeco Instruments Inc, USA). Then PDMS (Sylgard 184, USA) was poured, degassed, and cured using SU-8 as the master mold. For the oocyte chip, the cured PDMS was peeled from SU-8, followed by hole punching, oxygen plasma treatment and then bonded to the oxygen plasma treated glass slide. A separate valve device was made to control different flows in and out of the oocyte chip. Specifically, a silicone membrane (20 μm thickness, Wacker Chemie, Germany) was sandwiched between two PDMS layers as the valve. The upper PDMS layer (i.e., above the membrane) is connected to the pressure outputs (i.e., A, B, C, D in Figure 4) from the transistor chip. The lower PDMS layer is connected to different inlets and outlets of the oocyte chip.

For the 4-layer microfluidic transistor chip in Figure 4, a 1.2-mm biopsy punch was first used to punch out appropriate holes in layer 0, 1, and 2 PDMS. Then layer 1 PDMS was bonded to the silicone membrane (20 μm thickness, Wacker Chemie, Germany) using oxygen plasma treatment. A 1.2-mm biopsy punch was then used to punch through the silicone membrane to create shared ports (in amber color in Figures 3 and 4) with layer 2 PDMS. Next, the layer 1 PDMS – silicone membrane assembly was bonded to layer 2 PDMS following oxygen plasma treatment. Finally, layer 0 and layer 3 PDMS were similarly bonded to the layer 1 PDMS – silicone membrane – layer 2 PDMS assembly. A detailed schematic is included in Figure S3.

### Fluidic timer circuit modelling

To model the fluidic capacitor used in this work, we considered a rigid container filled with air with initial pressure and volume as P 0 and V 0 , respectively. As shown in Figure 3B, the capacitor is connected to pressure supply of P s u p 1 through a resistor with resistance of R 1 . To solve the P C (i.e., the air pressure inside the rigid container) as a function of time, the following governing equations are considered to account for the varying capacitance over time: (1) P s u p 1 = Q t * R 1 + P C t ; (2) Q t = C * d P C ( t ) d t ; (3) C = d V C L ( t ) d P C ( t ) = - d V C ( t ) d P C ( t ) ; (4) V C ( t ) * P C ( t ) = V 0 * P 0 Plugging Eq 4 into Eq 3, we have: (5) C = V C ( t ) P C ( t ) = P 0 * V 0 ( P C ( t ) ) 2 ; where Q ( t ) is the flow through the resistor into the capacitor, C is the capacitance, V C L ( t ) is the liquid volume inside the rigid container, V C ( t ) is the air volume inside the rigid container, P C ( t ) is the pressure inside the rigid container.

For the constant capacitance model in Figure 3B, a constant capacitance value is calculated from Eq. 5 using the final equilibrium value of P C , which is P s u p 1 .

### Fluidic timer circuit measurements

To measure P C in Figure 3B, a 40 cm-long peek tubing with 0.01-inch inner diameter (IDEX-HS) was used as the resistor. To create a rigid sealed container as the capacitor, the plunger of a 1 mL syringe was pulled to the position of 0.7 mL and then glued to the syringe wall. A 200 kPa pressure supply was provided using a computer-controlled pressure source (FlowEZ, Fluigent). The pressure at P C was measured using a pressure sensor (ABPDRRV015PDAA5, Honeywell).

To measure P o u t in Figures 3A & C, two pressure supplies were set to 200 kPa ( P s u p 1 ) and 180 kPa ( P s u p 2 ), respectively. Different air volumes were used as the capacitor and P o u t was recorded. Unless otherwise specified, all reservoirs for the pressure sources (P-CAP, Fluigent) were filled with 1× phosphate-buffered saline (Fisher Scientific).

### Logic gate circuit measurement

For the measurement of time-dependent digital pressure outputs in Figure 4, three pressure supplies were set to 200 kPa ( P s u p 1 ), 180 kPa ( P s u p 2 ) and 170 kPa (Psup3), respectively. A 15 cm-long 0.02-inch inner diameter Tygon tubing served as R2 shown in Figure 4A. Regarding capacitors, syringes with 0.6, 3.7, and 3.9 mL air were used for C2, C1, and C3, respectively. The 4-layer PDMS device was primed with PBS. The pressure values of ports A, B, C, and D were recorded.

### Linear CPA concentration profile

To create a linear CPA concentration profile from a constant pressure supply, the RC charging circuit and serpentine mixer were employed as shown in Figure 5B. The resistors R3, R4, and R5 are 6 cm, 10 cm and 50 cm long 0.01 inch inner diameter tubing, respectively. A syringe with 4 mL air was used as the capacitor (i.e., C4 in Figure 5B). The ES is 15% EG + 15% DMSO prepared in KSOMaa Evolve w/HEPES medium (LifeGlobal Group). The pressure supply (Psup4) was set to 30 kPa. To visualize the mixing of ES and media in the serpentine mixer, 0.1 mg/mL rhodamine B was added to the media for fluorescent imaging using an upright microscope (Nikon Eclipse 90i). The flow rates of each flow into and out of the oocyte chip were measured using Sensirion flow meters (SLI-1000).

### Numerical simulation

LTspice was used to simulate the circuit in Figure 5B. Fluidic to electric domain conversions are as follows: Pressure: 1 kPa = 1 Volt, Resistance: 1 kPa*s/uL = 1 ohm, Flow rate: 1 uL/s = 1 amp, Capacitance: 1 uL/kPa = 1 farad. The resistance of the mixer channel is estimated to increase linearly with the flow rate ratio of ES to media. A small nonzero source pressure for t < 200 s, which is the pressure resultant of imperfect valve seals, results in the capacitor having an initial charge and less reverse flow across R3 at the beginning of step 2. A 3D laminar flow model (Comsol 4.4) was built to simulate the laminar flow fields of the oocyte chip. Specifically, the 3D geometry of the oocyte chip was imported into Comsol. To simulate the flow conditions for oocyte trapping, the flow rate of the oocyte inlet was set to 90 μL/min, the pressure of the waste outlet was set to 0. No-slip wall conditions were applied. The fluidic properties of PBS were used (i.e., density of 1 g/mL, viscosity of 0.9 mPa*s). Built-in physics-controlled mesh for laminar flow was used.

### Autonomous CPA loading into the mouse oocyte

Frozen mouse MII oocytes were purchased from Embryotech laboratories (Haverhill, MA) and thawed as instructed by the vendor. As demonstrated by Mazur et al., vitrified-thawed oocytes can be considered as the equivalent to fresh oocytes in terms of verification of CPA loading.44–46 The thawed oocytes were cultured in KSOMaa Evolve w/HEPES medium at 37 °C and 5% CO2 for up to 3 hrs for recovery prior to the experiments and showed normal appearance under the inverted microscope (Figure S14). To load the oocyte into the oocyte chip, individual oocyte was first transferred into a pipette tip with 135 microns inner diameter (EZ-Tip, Cooper Surgical) under the microscope. The pipette tip was then inserted into a 1/32 inch inner diameter Tygon tubing which is connected to a Tee tubing junction connector (McMaster-Carr). The other two ports of the Tee connector were connected to a tubing from the media reservoir and a tubing to the oocyte inlet of the oocyte chip. After injecting 10 μL suspension containing the selected oocyte from the pipette to the tubing leading to the oocyte inlet of the oocyte chip, the pipette tip was clamped at the other end. The oocyte now can be pushed into the oocyte chip by the flow from the media reservoir when pressurized. The sequence of different actions including oocyte loading & trapping, linear loading of 7.5% EG + 7.5% DMSO in 15 min, subsequent loading of VS and oocyte collection were performed automatically. We performed 5 experimental repeats for each oocyte CPA loading condition, including 15 min linear loading, 15 min step loading and 10 min linear loading. Videos of the oocyte were recorded with an upright microscope under 10x objective (Nikon Eclipse 90i). To retrieve the oocyte after VS exposure, a tubing with 0.02’ ID was connected to the oocyte collection outlet of the oocyte chip. The other end of the tubing was placed on a nylon mesh with 20 μm pore size. An absorbent material was placed beneath the nylon mesh to drain the VS, while the oocyte stayed above the nylon mesh and was exposed to VS for the designed time (Figure S15).

### Oocyte staining

For live/dead staining, oocytes were incubated with 10 μg/ml Hoechst and 10 μg/ml propidium iodide (PI) for 15 minutes in dark. Pictures were taken with a Nikon Ti2 inverted microscope. To stain the spindle, oocytes were fixed in 3% paraformaldehyde freshly prepared in PBS for 25 minutes at room temperature, then permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS for 20 minutes, prior to incubation in blocking solution (1% BSA, 0.1% Tween 20 in PBS) for 1 hr. Primary mouse anti α-tubulin antibody (Cell Signaling, 3873T, 1:200) was added in blocking solution and incubated with the oocytes overnight at 4 °C. Next, the oocytes were washed with washing buffer (0.1% Tween 20 in PBS) for 3 times (8 minutes each time). Secondary antibodies (goat anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 647, ThermoFisher, A-21235) were added (1:1000) and incubated for 1 hr at room temperature. The oocytes were then washed 3 times with the washing buffer. Hoechst was added (final concentration 10 μg/ml) and incubated for 15 minutes. The oocytes were placed in a glass bottom petri dish (MatTek Life Science) and imaged with a confocal microscope using 20x objectives (Nikon A1R).
